courses.subject: DIPL
courses.title: Political Psychology for Diplomacy and International Relations
courses.description: This is a course focusing on those areas of political psychology most relevant to diplomacy and international relations. As such, we will start with an introduction to political psychology as its own interdisciplinary field: the study of psychological phenomena in politics or politically relevant features of psychology. Then we will cover key foundations of the relevant psychology, like social psychological biases, System 1 and 2 thought, and motivated cognition. Next we’ll explore important areas of political psychology, from system justification to moral reasoning. Then, we’ll delve into some applications of political psychology to international relations, and conclude with a bit of economic psychology of broad relevance. By the end, you should have a general grasp of political psychology as a field, and be able to incorporate psychological knowledge into your understanding of international relations and diplomacy.
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course, students are expected to
1) Understand how features of human social and individual psychology affect political cognition, influencing how politics operates on a national scale as well as within the global political-economic system.
2) Be conversant with key psychological biases, how they operate, their evolutionary origins, and how culture may affect them.
3) Be able to appraise psychological studies and make judgments about their applicability to political-economic issues.
4) Understand the evidence provided within scientific articles, grasp the methods used, and critically evaluate their conclusions.

courses.subject: DIPL
courses.title: Summer Course
courses.description: This course is tailored for students majoring in Diplomacy and International Studies. It aims to offer a deep dive into China’s changing international relationships and the significant domestic and global factors shaping its policy making. Students will travel to a different city to analyse China’s foreign affairs in today’s international system. Prior to the trip, students will participate in preparatory seminars to gain essential background knowledge of international and China’s political economy, geopolitics, and development issues, as well as to learn basic field research methods. Through on-site visits and guided interactions, students will apply theoretical frameworks to real-world contexts and develop practical skills in diplomacy and international studies. After the fieldwork visits, students will design and undertake a research project that connects their field observations with academic analysis.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

* Demonstrate an informed understanding of the political, economic, and social characteristics and foreign policies of the region visited.
* Apply relevant theories and concepts from international studies to interpret field observations.
* Design and carry out a concise research project addressing a specific question related to the field experience.
* Critically reflect on what has been learnt, articulating the connections between academic knowledge and practical, real-world encounters.
courses.course_syllabus:
Pre-Departure Seminars (3 sessions, 3 hours each):

* Introduction to diplomacy in the Chinese context: political system, economic landscape, and historical background
* Design a research topic
* Research methods for field studies: question formulation, observation, data collection, and ethical considerations
* Research project design: formulating research questions based on field observations and data gathering

Field Study (variable duration):

* Visits to academic institutions, international organizations, multinational corporations and governmental offices
* Thematic briefings and discussions on topics such as geopolitical trends, economic development, governance, foreign policy, and social issues in the region
* Interactive sessions with local experts and practitioners

Post-Fieldwork Activities:

* There will be a de-briefing session for students to share their experiences
* Data analysis and synthesis of field findings and archive data
* A post-trip seminar will be held to discuss various student reports
* Writing of a research report connecting field experience with academic frameworks

courses.title: Navigating Conflict: Mediation and Dispute Resolution in Social Contexts
courses.description:
This 13-week undergraduate course offers a comprehensive introduction to the principles, theories, and practices of mediation and dispute resolution within a social science framework. Drawing on insights from sociology, psychology, conflict studies, and cultural anthropology, the course examines how disputes emerge in a wide range of settings—including interpersonal, community, and institutional environments.

A central focus is placed on culturally sensitive approaches to mediation, with specific relevance to Hong Kong and the broader Asian context. Students are encouraged to critically engage with both local and international perspectives on conflict resolution, developing an awareness of how social and cultural factors influence dispute dynamics and outcomes.

Through a blend of experiential learning—such as role-playing simulations, case analyses, and reflective exercises—students will gain practical skills that prepare them for successful careers in social work, community organization, human resources, or advanced studies in conflict resolution. Importantly, this course directly aligns with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 16: Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions. By fostering expertise in peaceful dispute resolution and promoting inclusive, participatory methods of conflict management, the course equips students to contribute meaningfully to just and sustainable societies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students should be able to
1. Explain and differentiate key theories and models of conflict and dispute resolution, demonstrating a foundational understanding of their application within social science.
2. Apply mediation techniques in simulated role-plays, effectively considering and integrating relevant cultural and social dynamics—particularly those unique to Hong Kong and Asian contexts.
3. Analyze real-world disputes using social science perspectives, with particular attention to power imbalances, cultural diversity, and ethical considerations influencing conflict dynamics.
4. Critically assess the effectiveness of mediation across diverse scenarios—including family, workplace, and community disputes—by evaluating case studies specific to both local and international contexts.
5. Demonstrate advanced communication and facilitation skills required for neutral third-party intervention, including active listening, reframing, and consensus-building, to foster peaceful and sustainable outcomes.

courses.subject: DIPL
courses.title: Human Rights and Global Security in International Relations
courses.description:
This module offers an in-depth comparative analysis of the relationship between human rights and global security within the framework of international relations. By adopting a legal perspective, this course will engage with key jurisprudential theories, legal frameworks, statutory provisions and practical legal enforcement experience that underpin major geopolitical entities, including China (both Chinese mainland and Hong Kong), the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and Middle Eastern countries.

In particular, this course will explore the evolution and interpretation of national security laws and human rights protections across different legal systems, address the impact of major national security events on domestic and international legal norms, examine the reciprocal influence between changes of national security legislations and developments in international relations, and understand the role of domestic institutions (including the executive government, the legislature and the judiciary) and international organisations in mediating the balance between national security and human rights.

By the end of the course, students will develop a nuanced understanding of how legal responses to national security challenges can both drive and reflect broader transformations in global governance and international relations.
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1: Introduction to the Comparative Legal Perspective of Security and Human Rights
This session will introduce the module’s aims, structure and expectations. It will define the concepts of global security and human rights within international relations, explore the historical and conceptual tensions between national security imperatives and human rights protections, and understand the significance of adopting a legal perspective in analyzing these issues.

Week 2: Foundations and Sources of International and National Human Rights

This session will introduce the fundamental sources of international human rights law, including key treaties, customary international law, general principles of law, and soft law instruments such as declarations and guidelines. It will also cover how these international legal obligations are implemented domestically through constitutions, legislations, and judicial decisions. Additionally, the session will provide an introduction to the foundations of national security law, exploring its legal basis, scope, and how it interacts with human rights protections.

Week 3: Jurisprudential Theories and Legal Frameworks of Balancing Security and Rights
This week’s content explores the theoretical and legal foundations that guide national institutions (including the executive, the legislature and the judiciary) in making decisions that balance the often-competing pursuits of national security imperatives and human rights protections. This session will assess the extent to which restrictions on rights can be justified by legitimate security objectives, applying principles such as proportionality, necessity and legality.

Week 4: National Security Laws and Human Rights in the United States
This week will provide an in-depth examination of the U.S. legal framework governing national security and its relationship with human rights protections. The session will begin by discussing the constitutional distribution of national security powers among the three branches of government, highlighting the President’s authority in matters of war and security, Congress’s role in authorizing the use of force, and the courts’ oversight functions. Landmark cases such as Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer will be analyzed to illustrate the limits and scope of executive power. It will also discuss how the national security laws and human rights protections in the United States have both influenced and been influenced by international relations.

Week 5: National Security Laws and Human Rights in the United Kingdom
This week will provide a comprehensive examination of the UK’s national security legal framework and its interaction with human rights protections. This session will begin with an overview of the national security strategy of the UK and will explore key legislations underpinning UK national security, including the National Security Act 2023, Terrorism Acts 2000 and 2006 and the Official Secrets Act 1989 and the recent laws on investigatory powers such as the Investigatory Powers (Amendment) Act 2024. The balance between effective security measures and human rights protections, and the relationship between national security and international relations will be critically examined.

Week 6: European Union: Human Rights and Security Policies
This week will explore the European Union’s approach to balancing human rights and security policies within its internal and external frameworks. The session will begin by examining the EU’s human rights priorities, and will analyze the EU’s evolving security laws and policies, focusing on the 2025 strategic initiatives to strengthen the European Defence Union, enhance cooperation with NATO and global partners, and transition from reactive to proactive security through the Preparedness Union Strategy and the European Internal Security Strategy. It will also examine how these developments have been both driven by and influential upon international and transnational relations.

Week 7: Middle East: Security Challenges and Human Rights in Conflict Zones
This week will provide a comprehensive analysis of the security challenges facing the Middle East and their implications for human rights in conflict-affected zones. The session will begin by outlining the region’s volatile geopolitical landscape, political instability, and shifting power dynamics. Key flashpoints include the regional tensions involving Iran, Israel, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, and other states. The session will also consider the national security laws and policies that have resulted from these conflicts, alongside their accompanying human rights consequences.

Week 8: International Institutions and Mechanisms Mediating Security and Human Rights
This week will focus on the role of international institutions and mechanisms in mediating the relationship between security and human rights. The session will explore how multilateral organizations, legal frameworks, and mediation bodies contribute to the peaceful resolution of disputes, conflict prevention, and the protection of human rights in situations of insecurity. Particular attention will be given to explore why these international and transnational organisations and legal framework succeed and fail in balancing national security interests with human rights, while respecting the sovereignty and autonomy of individual states.

Week 9: National Security Laws and Human Rights in China
This session will examine the historical development of national security theories, strategies, laws, and practices in mainland China. It will provide a historical overview of the evolution of national security concepts, focusing on the formulation of the holistic national security framework introduced in 2014 and the subsequent enactment of the National Security Law of the People’s Republic of China in 2015. Building on this foundation, the session will evaluate the relationship between the 2015 National Security Law and other relevant national security legislation in the PRC. Additionally, it will explore how China’s national security strategies, policies, and laws have been balanced against human rights considerations and shaped by the dynamics of international relations.

Week 10: National Security Laws and Human Rights in Hong Kong
This session will examine the development of national security laws in Hong Kong, focusing on the enactment of the Hong Kong National Security Law and the domestic implementation of Article 23 of the Hong Kong Basic Law through the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance. It will explore how Hong Kong’s government, Legislative Council, and courts have sought to balance national security imperatives with human rights protections within the framework of “One Country, Two Systems”. The session will also evaluate the influence of mainland China’s political directives and the international community’s responses on the formulation, interpretation, and enforcement of Hong Kong’s national security laws and their impact on human rights.

Week 11: Group Presentations and Discussions
Group presentations on selected topics with Q&A sessions.

Week 12: Contemporary Challenges and Future Directions of a Balanced Protection of Securities and Human Rights
This week will focus on the evolving challenges of achieving a balanced protection of national security and human rights, drawing on recent developments and ongoing global debates. The session will critically examine the implications of national security and human rights considerations in international relations, exploring the tensions, trade-offs, and potential pathways to reconcile these often-competing imperatives in both domestic and international contexts.

Week 13: Conclusion and End of Term Essay Preparation

courses.subject: DIPL
courses.title: Internship
courses.description:
This aim of this course is to provide students with opportunities to observe the management operations in the business, public sector or non-government organizations (NGOs) in Hong Kong or beyond, and to experience the work life in the sector, as well as to nurture students’ global vision.

It is recommended that the internship to be conducted from June to August after finishing year three studies in the block mode (i.e. 5 days x 8 hours x 6 weeks). However, in case of special circumstances, students may also choose the ‘distributed mode’ (i.e. several hours in a week over a number of weeks equalling 240 hours). DIPL Programme will deploy work units, agencies, or organizations that provide internships relevant to the general course objectives. Meanwhile, students are encouraged to explore opportunities of internship to fit their own specific learning needs. However, all self-selected internship must comply with the course requirements (including the duration and nature of the internship), and subjected to the approval of DIPL Programme Director. Guidance and assistance will be provided whenever appropriate.

During the internship, each student would be guided and assisted by an academic supervisor. The supervisor offers advice and help whenever necessary during the attachment period. At the same time, each student will be receiving guidance and assistance from his/her agency supervisor. Students will construct and submit a portfolio to reflect on the experience in the internship. Academic advice will be provided to help students consolidate their learning in the internship.

courses.subject: DIPL
courses.title: Capstone Project
courses.description: The aim of this course is to provide students with learning opportunities to undertake a final Capstone Project before graduation. Students are required to form groups and design a project on selected topics related to current global affairs or diplomatic issues under the supervision of a faculty member. Students need to integrate and apply knowledge and techniques from their courses, overseas exchange, and internships to develop and complete a real-world analytical and diplomatic project. Students are encouraged to think out of the box and can submit their projects in any format such as a development project, video, website as agreed upon with their supervisor.
